passages.heading: The core idea
passages.markdown: Security controls reduce risk at different boundaries. A locked equipment room limits physical access, while an account permission limits what a signed-in user can do. Cameras can help detect and investigate events but do not physically prevent entry by themselves. Layered protection combines preventive, detective, and corrective measures so one control’s failure does not remove every defense. Choose controls that address an actual threat rather than adding complexity without a purpose.

passages.heading: In the real world
passages.markdown: The principle of least privilege grants only the access needed for a task. Multifactor authentication combines different factor types, such as something known and something possessed; two passwords are still the same factor type. Single sign-on reduces repeated sign-ins across applications but needs careful account protection. Just-in-time privileged access limits how long elevated permissions remain available. Zero Trust evaluates access explicitly instead of treating a network location as proof of trust. Review access when roles change, remove unused permissions, and retain useful records for investigation.

passages.heading: Make it stick
passages.markdown: Put it into practice by explaining the decision in your own words. In a support scenario, identify the requirement first, connect it to the relevant technology, and check the result against that requirement. If the evidence changes, revisit your reasoning rather than repeating the same action. Document what you observed so the next person can understand your conclusion.
